facts.statement: The genus Septencoracias was described by Bourdon and colleagues in 2016.
facts.quote: authority: Bourdon et al., 2016

facts.statement: The genus contains two species: the type species Septencoracias morsensis described in 2016 and S. simillimus named in 2024.
facts.quote: It contains two species, Septencoracias morsensis described in 2016, and S. simillimus, which was named in 2024.

facts.statement: Fossils of Septencoracias date to the Ypresian stage of the Early Eocene, approximately 54 million years ago.
facts.quote: It was found in the Fur Formation of Denmark, dating back to the Ypresian of the Lower Eocene Epoch, about 54 million years ago.

facts.statement: Septencoracias is an extinct bird related to modern rollers and other members of the order Coraciiformes.
facts.quote: Septencoracias is an extinct genus of bird related to modern rollers and other Coraciiformes such as kingfishers, bee-eaters, motmots, and todies.

facts.statement: Septencoracias was a small bird approximately 25 cm in length, similar in size to a Northern carmine bee-eater.
facts.quote: Septencoracias was a small bird the size of a Northern carmine bee-eater, Merops nubicus, about 25 cm in length.

facts.statement: The skull of Septencoracias was large relative to its body, measuring about twice the length of its humerus.
facts.quote: It had a large skull in comparison to its body, about twice the length of the humerus.

facts.statement: Septencoracias possessed a stout, slightly curved beak with an upper ridge that curved gradually toward the tip, similar to modern rollers.
facts.quote: It had a stout, slightly curved beak, and the upper ridge of the beak curves gradually towards the tip of the bill like in living roller species.

facts.statement: Septencoracias had small, egg-shaped nasal openings, distinct from the elongated, slit-like, or triangular nares found in its relatives and modern rollers.
facts.quote: It had small, egg-shaped nasal openings, much different than any of its close extinct relatives or extant rollers, which have either elongated openings, slit-like openings, or large triangular nares.

facts.statement: The single known fossil specimen lacks the sternum and most of the shoulder girdle, except for a left scapula that was not bifurcated like in later rollers.
facts.quote: The only fossil specimen of Septencoracias does not preserve the sternum and shoulder girdle, except for the left scapula, which is not bifurcated as in Late Eocene and later rollers.

facts.statement: Septencoracias retained a small claw on its alular digit, a feature usually absent in modern birds but shared with its relative Primobucco.
facts.quote: Like in Primobucco, Septencoracias has a small claw on its alular digit, which is usually absent in modern birds.

facts.statement: Septencoracias had a very wide pelvis and hind limb proportions similar to those of modern rollers.
facts.quote: Septencoracias had a very wide pelvis, and had similar proportions in its hind limbs as modern rollers.

facts.statement: It is uncertain whether Septencoracias exhibited syndactyly (fusion of toes three and four), a condition common in modern Coraciiformes.
facts.quote: Though most modern Coraciiformes show syndactyly, with three forward-pointing toes and toes three and four fused at the base, Septencoracias is not entirely certain to have this condition.

facts.statement: Fossil remains of Septencoracias show soft tissue preservation, primarily within the thoracic and abdominal cavities.
facts.quote: The fossil remains show soft tissue preservation, mostly in the thoracic and abdominal cavities, though portions were also seen in the skull.

facts.statement: The type specimen was discovered in the Moclay Pit on the Island of Mors in Jutland, Denmark.
facts.quote: It was discovered in the Moclay Pit on the Island of Mors, in Jutland, Denmark, in the Fur Formation.

facts.statement: The genus name Septencoracias combines 'septentrio' (meaning north) with the name of modern rollers, Coracias.
facts.quote: The genus name stems from 'septentrio', meaning north, and the genus name of many modern rollers, Coracias.

facts.statement: The specific name morsensis refers to the Island of Mors where the fossil was found.
facts.quote: The specific name stems from the Island of Mors.

facts.statement: An additional specimen from the Tielt Formation in Belgium was tentatively identified as Septencoracias in 2019.
facts.quote: An additional specimen from the Tielt Formation in Egem, Belgium was referred to cf. Septencoracias sp. in 2019.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analysis in 2016 identified Septencoracias as the sister taxon of Primobucco.
facts.quote: A phylogenetic analysis in 2016 recovered Septencoracias as the sister taxon of Primobucco.

facts.statement: Septencoracias is the oldest known member of the Coraciiformes, indicating the group was already diversified by the Early Eocene.
facts.quote: Septencoracias is the oldest known member of the Coraciiformes, so it shows that this group was already fairly diversified by the Early Eocene, following the end-Cretaceous extinction.

facts.statement: Fish remains, specifically argentinoids about 10 cm long, were found in the gut of the Septencoracias specimen.
facts.quote: It was found with fish remains in its gut, of a very common taxon from the Fur Formation, argentinoids of about 10 cm in length.

facts.statement: The presence of fish in its gut suggests early Coraciiformes had a more varied diet than modern species, which mostly eat insects and small land vertebrates.
facts.quote: This contributes to the idea that early roller and roller relatives had a much more varied diet than modern members of the group, which almost exclusively feed upon insects and small land vertebrates.

facts.statement: Septencoracias fossils are from the Eastern Hemisphere, the region where all modern rollers currently live.
facts.quote: Septencoracias was found in the Eastern Hemisphere, which is where all modern rollers are found, though they all occur in modern tropical and subtropical regions.

facts.statement: The discovery of Septencoracias in Denmark suggests that early Coraciiformes had a much wider range in the Northern Hemisphere during the warm Eocene climate.
facts.quote: Given the warmer climate of the Eocene, the finding of Septencoracias in Denmark indicates that the range of early Coraciiformes was much wider within the Northern Hemisphere during this time, due to the increased number of suitable habitats.

facts.statement: The time range for Septencoracias is estimated from 56 to 48.07 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Ypresian to Ypresian (56 to 48.07 million years ago)

rejected.statement: The fossil was discovered during a geology field course in an abandoned diatomite quarry.
rejected.quote: It was found during a geology field course in an abandoned diatomite quarry.

rejected.statement: Despite finding fish in its gut, Septencoracias likely mostly fed on insects and small land vertebrates as it was a terrestrial bird.
rejected.quote: However, Septencoracias probably mostly fed on insects and small land vertebrates, similar to its modern relatives, given that it was a terrestrial bird.
